title: ADM-160 Miniature Air Launched Decoy Wreckage A Reminder Of Ongoing Spying On Iran’s Air Defenses
body: Remnants claimed to be photographed in Iran have been identified as belonging to a Raytheon ADM-160 Miniature Air-Launched Decoy (MALD). The wreckage was reportedly recovered after an Iranian interception that occurred earlier in the day, although the exact location and circumstances remain unconfirmed and there is reason for caution. Iranian state and military media have a long record of presenting unverified or exaggerated claims , especially during periods of conflict, and imagery released through those channels warrants independent scrutiny. Still, the MALD identification appears credible based on the visible wreckage, but its provenance, location, and the circumstances of its loss have not yet been independently established. MALDs were likely used at least in the opening stages of Operation Epic Fury, as well. With that being said, the showing off of the MALD wreckage, regardless of its original use case, is something of a reminder that U.S. and Israeli forces are continuing to evaluate Iran’s electronic order of battle, which can include probing activities that leverage deception and decoys to better understand the state of Iran’s air defenses and command and control architecture. This is critical information that needs to be constantly updated for contingency and future potential air campaign purposes. Wreckage of the MALD. Iranian media Iranian sources today reported the destruction of an Orbiter-type reconnaissance drone over the Strait of Hormuz, before the separate imagery emerged showing what appears to be the wreckage of a MALD. It is not yet clear whether the two reports refer to the same incident or separate losses. A close-up of the wreckage of the MALD. Iranian media The appearance of the wreckage could also shed a light on how the U.S. and Israel can conduct ongoing air operations against Iran, even if kinetic actions have largely slowed to a trickle. 15090 is the CAGE code for Raytheon, which is visible on the tail fins and other remnants. Source for images: https://t.co/weIo1Hh6RR pic.twitter.com/4LoBMChKZG — Trevor Ball (@Easybakeovensz) September 20, 2026 MALD is an expendable store, launched from another aircraft. The ADM-160 family was developed to provide a flexible way of decoying and distracting an enemy’s air defenses, while also adding to the survivability of allied aircraft and standoff weapons. Raytheon won the U.S. Air Force development contract for the current-generation ADM-160B in 2003. The B design is significantly different from the initial A-model from Teledyne Ryan (later Northrop Grumman), the development of which had started in the late 1990s . The B also features a more powerful turbojet engine and possesses greater range. MALDs being prepared for loading onto an aircraft. U.S. Air Force The ADM-160B is approximately 6.5 feet long, has a wingspan of roughly 5.6 feet when deployed, and is powered by a small turbojet. It has an operational range of around 550 miles. Rather than carrying a conventional warhead, the MALD carries equipment intended to reproduce the radar signature of specific aircraft or standoff weapons. It can therefore provide additional and often highly enticing tracks for an adversary’s radar operators and surface-to-air missile crews to respond to. It can be programmed to fly intricate routes to better rival the target it is emulating and to provoke the attention of air defenders. The related ADM-160C MALD-J adds an electronic warfare capability, allowing it to perform stand-in jamming and other forms of active electronic attacks against enemy air defense nodes. Further improved variants of the MALD, which the U.S. Navy has also been acquiring, have since been developed as you can read more about here . The exact variant involved in today’s incident cannot be established from all publicly available imagery at this stage. An ADM-160B under the wing of a U.S. Air Force B-52 bomber. U.S. Air Force The possibility that the United States had used MALDs against Iran had already attracted considerable attention following Operation Midnight Hammer , the U.S. strike against Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. During the operation, U.S. officials described a complex deception plan involving aircraft and other decoy measures designed to prevent Iran from determining the true direction and composition of the attack. This strongly pointed to MALD as one likely component of that deception architecture. The opening hours and days of Operation Epic Fury also likely saw MALD employments. ADM-160s have also been used extensively by Ukraine against Russia, primarily for provoking air defense systems into radiating and as penetration aids for cruise missiles. In the Strait of Hormuz context, the MALD could serve a dual purpose. It could act in its primary role, as a defensive measure for allied aircraft and standoff weapons, drawing Iranian air defense systems away from it and toward the decoy. It can also be used more independently, triggering Iranian defenses and revealing their locations and operating characteristics, as well as the state of Iran’s command and control for those assets. Surveillance platforms, especially those in the air, can then soak up all that signals data. This can then be used to generate intelligence for future operations, and all without putting a person or an expensive piece of equipment at risk. The unique nature of the current state of the Iran conflict would allow for MALD to be used in this unique manner. While kinetic actions have become sporadic, they are still occurring, so firing a decoy that looks like something much more threatening to Iranian air defenders would not be an unprecedented escalation. An ADM-160 MALD in flight. Raytheon Iran has characterized the incident as a shoot-down. If Iranian forces did successfully engage the MALD, that would represent a real air defense interception of a U.S. deception system, although these are expendable by design. It is equally possible that the MALD malfunctioned or just flew its route and ran out of fuel and crashed, as designed. The wreckage also does not, by itself, identify the aircraft that launched the MALD. The system has been integrated with a broad range of U.S. aircraft. In the course of U.S. operations against Iran, we have notably seen Air Force A-10C Thunderbolt II attack jets returning from theater with markings depicting MALD missions . An A-10 with mission marks showing a mix of weapons used against Iranian targets. They include MALDs, Small Diameter Bombs, GBU-12 Paveways, Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) laser-guided rockets, AGM-65 Maverick air-to-surface missiles, and generic bombs that probably signify Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAMs). Andrew McKelvey It is also worth noting that the MALD wreckage has appeared at the same time as reports of unusual, UAP-like objects over Iran, with videos and eyewitness accounts circulating online. Their authenticity and nature remain unclear. A number of videos are circulating showing an unidentified object in the skies above Tehran, Iran, it’s not immediately clear what is being filmed. pic.twitter.com/bHNAQGFPNv — OSINTdefender (@sentdefender) September 21, 2026 Such reports come amid an increasingly sophisticated use of low-end drones , decoys, and other forms of deception. These kinds of systems can be employed not only to stimulate adversary air defenses, but also to distract populations and probe how information moves out of a denied area. In such an environment, unusual aerial sightings should be viewed with caution — but not necessarily dismissed as irrelevant. We have been talking about how new forms of misdirection and guile will leverage relatively low-end technologies in future conflicts for many years now. While it isn’t clear if this light show in the sky over Iran was such an activity, it is certainly a reminder to keep that possibility in mind. I don’t know what this is, or if it’s legit BUT remember we are in a new age of misdirection, decoy and guile. Specifically using low end drone technology. There are more ways to stimulate an enemy air defense system, distract a populous, assess the flow of public info from a… https://t.co/wW7YVlbayB — Tyler Rogoway (@Aviation_Intel) September 21, 2026 Meanwhile, the prospect of renewed U.S. strikes is increasingly being raised on both sides. Iran’s central military command said Sunday that it had received information that Washington was preparing to resume attacks, while President Donald Trump told Fox News that he was in a “deciding mode” and was considering further military action alongside economic pressure and a deal. Trump had also told Axios last week that he was approaching a major decision on whether to resume large-scale military operations, with U.S. forces in the region being maintained at current levels through the end of the year. Iranian officials have warned that a renewed U.S. attack would trigger retaliation against American forces and interests across the region. At the same time, Qatar and Pakistan are pursuing diplomatic efforts to restart negotiations. This situation is exactly why keeping as detailed intelligence on the status of Iran’s air defense overlay would be so critical. Building a highly detailed electronic order of battle and maintaining it is critical to the effectiveness of future air operations. There is usually an observable burst of such activity prior to a major operation kicking off, as well. There are also many unseen assets that help with this, from those in space to those in the air and even those under the sea. There have been reports of Israel’s secretive RA-01 stealth flying wing drone being spotted over Iran and of course the U.S. has its own RQ-170 and RQ-180 aircraft, just to name a couple known penetrating assets that are likely highly capable of collecting this information. Regardless, the U.S. and Israel will have a lot of ‘maintenance’ to do in order to roll back any air defense capabilities Iran has been able to reconstitute should hostilities break out in full again, and a lot of critical intelligence data will need to be up-to-date in order to support such an operation. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post ADM-160 Miniature Air Launched Decoy Wreckage A Reminder Of Ongoing Spying On Iran’s Air Defenses appeared first on TWZ .

title: Rosoboronexport exhibits new Strike Drones at the Egypt Airshow
body: Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport , publicly displayed two new air-launched weapons, the S-71M and S-71K, alongside the Su-57E stealth fighter at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt from September 8 to 10, 2026. The event marked the Su-57E’s first appearance at an African air show and the first public showing of both weapons. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi opened the second edition of the show at El Alamein International Airport on September 8. Organizers, including Egypt’s Ministry of Defence , the Egyptian Air Force and the Egyptian Space Agency, drew more than 250 exhibitors from roughly 50 countries, according to a Russian state broadcaster. Flight demonstrations included Egypt’s Silver Stars, Saudi Arabia’s Saudi Hawks, and the Su-57. A Rosoboronexport representative, speaking to Reuters on condition of anonymity, said the S-71M and S-71K had already seen combat use. Describing the weapons, he told the news agency: “It’s not a drone, it’s not a missile, it’s something (like) both”. Industry publications cited by Reuters describe the pair as combining features of cruise missiles and low-cost attack drones. United Aircraft Corporation (UAC), the Rostec subsidiary that builds the Su-57, identified the S-71M as a warhead-delivery platform and the S-71K as an aviation bomb. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Agency has said the S-71K, known as “Kovyor” or “Kover”, carries an OFAB-250-270 warhead and lacks terminal guidance, making it a low-cost, stand-off weapon rather than a precision-strike system. Its flattened airframe and forward-mounted wings are designed to reduce the missile’s radar return, giving it a measure of low observability. The S-71M, called “Monokhrom”, is described by UAC and Defense outlets as a more autonomous follow-on design. It carries an electro-optical seeker and has loitering capability, allowing it to search for and engage moving targets, with an operator able to confirm the target before impact. Both weapons are sized to fit the Su-57’s internal weapons bay, preserving the jet’s low-observable profile when armed. Rostec also showed the S8000 “Banderol” (developed by Kronshtadt Group), a smaller precision-guided missile that first emerged publicly in 2025 and has reportedly seen use in Russia’s war in Ukraine. Defense channels have put its range at roughly 500 km, with a maximum speed of 600 km per hour and a 150-kg warhead. Unlike the S-71 pair, the Banderol is built for multiple launch platforms, including fighters, the Mi-28 attack helicopter, and improvised ground launchers. The Su-57E is the export version of Russia’s only fifth-generation fighter, a single-seat, twin-engine aircraft with thrust-vectoring engines built to compete with Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II. Rosoboronexport’s static and flying displays paired the jet with the RVV-MD2 short-range and RVV-BD long-range air-to-air missiles, the Kh-38MLE air-to-surface missile, the Kh-69 low-observable cruise missile and the Kh-58UShKE anti-radiation missile. The export model has previously appeared at air shows in China , India and the United Arab Emirates, but El Alamein was its first outing in Africa. Russia ’s push for African and Middle Eastern buyers comes as the Su-57 program has struggled to close major export deals. Algeria has been widely reported as the aircraft’s first export customer, with two jets reportedly delivered to an unnamed buyer in late 2025. Ukraine has said its forces struck a Su-57 at a Russian air base in 2024, a claim Moscow has not addressed publicly. Rosoboronexport chief executive Alexander Mikheev said the agency holds new contracts tied to the Su-57E without naming customers or quantities. Russia’s Federal Service for Military-Technical Cooperation said 35 Russian organizations exhibited more than 500 military items at the show, spanning Almaz-Antey’s air defense systems, Tactical Missiles Corporation’s munitions and High-Precision Systems’ short-range weapons. The emergence of the S-71 family and the Banderol reflects a wider shift in Russian doctrine toward cheaper, expendable strike weapons that can be produced and fielded in volume. Officials and analysts tracking the war in Ukraine have said mass use of low-cost, radar-evading munitions has proven effective at wearing down layered air defenses, a lesson Moscow appears to be applying directly to its export catalog. Pairing such weapons with a fifth-generation platform like the Su-57E gives prospective buyers, many of them African and Middle Eastern air forces without their own stealth aircraft, a lower-cost path to the same tactical effect. China used the same show to display its J-16 fighter days after joint exercises with Egypt under the “Eagles of Civilization” banner, as the United States sent A-10, F-15E, F-16, and C-130 aircraft along with personnel from the Texas Air National Guard. Military delegations from Sierra Leone, Tanzania, and Kuwait were among the observers, an indication that the broader competition for African defense markets is now playing out at El Alamein. Rosoboronexport has not said when the S-71M and S-71K will be available for export or whether any foreign customer has placed an order. Further details are likely to surface as UAC and Rostec continue marketing the weapons to prospective buyers across Africa and the Middle East in the coming months.

title: NATO would strike back if Russia attacks, Polish FM says he warned Moscow
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski says he has personally warned Russian officials that Polish response to a possible attack from Moscow would include both offensive and defensive actions, according to an episode of the program Front Sikorskiego. Sikorski's disclosure comes as European governments step up preparations for possible Russian attacks and provocations. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on 17 September that intelligence assessments indicated Russia could stage drone or missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine in the coming months, while Lithuania said it had access to the same intelligence. Sikorski says he has told Russian officials to "be careful, because we have more combat aircraft than you do." "So if you do something that no one wants, we won't just sit back and do nothing. We will respond both defensively and offensively," Sikorski stresses. He frames the warning as deterrence and points to Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refining infrastructure as an example of what air power can achieve. Ukraine has destroyed what Sikorski described as 30–40% of Russia's oil refining capacity, he says, arguing that European air forces could accomplish far more. European governments prepare for Russian provocations Tusk said Russia could try to present such attacks as accidents in an effort to weaken NATO's willingness to respond. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys confirmed the following day that his country had the same intelligence and said officials had discussed the possibility of a Russian false-flag operation, according to Delfi. France has also moved to prepare for possible Russian hybrid attacks. President Emmanuel Macron ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and sensitive defense-industry sites from drone and cyberattacks, the Kyiv Independent reported , after saying the Russian hybrid threat had intensified. "The day we are attacked physically, we will not be warned," Macron said. Sikorski did not say when he delivered the warning or which Russian officials received it. title: Warning sirens are going west: Russian jet-powered drones bring strikes closer to NATO country
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Poland will have more than 1,000 automated warning sirens in Lublin Voivodeship by the end of 2026, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said on 19 September, up from nearly 350 now. The region had about 30 remotely activated sirens at the beginning of 2024. The expansion comes as Russian attacks on the west of Ukraine are reaching closer to Poland. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Russia is expected to intensify attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and warned of possible "accidental" drone or missile strikes on NATO countries, including Poland. He also said Russia is introducing jet-powered drones that move much faster and at higher altitudes. Sirens sound as drones approach the border A Russian air attack on western Ukraine triggered air-raid warnings in Poland's Lublin and Podkarpackie regions on 17 September. Sirens sounded in Lublin and Rzeszów, while residents received an SMS warning: "ATTENTION! ATTENTION! ATTENTION! Threat of an air attack. Find a safe place. Follow the instructions of the emergency services. Await further announcements." The Polish military said its aircraft were activated in response to Russian strikes involving jet-powered drones against western Ukraine. A Russian drone flying toward Poland fell on Ukrainian territory about four kilometers from the Polish border, according to Polish authorities. Polish airspace was not violated. Airports in Lublin and Rzeszów temporarily suspended operations to give military aircraft freedom of movement. Polish authorities said the measures were preventive and intended to protect Polish airspace. More strikes on the border zone On 13 September, Russian strikes near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing damaged a gas station and hit the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train about two kilometers from the Polish border. No deaths were reported, and the border crossing temporarily halted operations. On 19 September, Poland again activated ground-based air-defense systems and increased radar reconnaissance in response to another wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine. The operation ended the same day with no violation of Polish airspace recorded. Shelters, sirens, and a 1939 echo Beyond sirens, authorities have marked nearly 3,500 official shelter locations in Lublin Voivodeship. More than 500 State Fire Service stations and volunteer fire units took part in special exercises on 19 September to practice responses to warning signals and emergency alerts. " We are building a civil-protection system virtually from scratch," Kierwiński said at a briefing in Lublin. "We have very, very little time." The 17 September strikes fell on the anniversary of the Soviet Union's 1939 invasion of Poland. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the Russian attack as "massive, extremely brutal." The 13 September strikes near the border also drew a response from Kyiv. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described them as Putin's terror "knocking" directly on the doors of the EU and NATO and called for a "full trade embargo, a total entry ban, and complete sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex." title: Russia’s threat isn’t better missile, it’s 14,000 cheap ones. Its new deadly weapon was built in early 1990s, experts say
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia wants to build 14,000 of a new cruise missile next year, enough to fire them at Ukrainian cities by the thousand. The weapon, the Dan-T, is a cheap air-launched jet missile that flies hundreds of kilometers on its own, RBC-Ukraine reported . The danger is volume, not finesse. Russia aims to produce up to 2,000 Dan-T missiles by the end of this year and scale it drastically, RBC-Ukraine's sources say. Fired in large numbers, it would add a fresh layer to the Gerans and the cruise and ballistic missiles that already saturate Ukraine's skies on the worst nights. Numbers make the threat The experts are less worried about any single Dan-T than about the swarm. High speed, long range, and the ability to launch the missiles by the thousand would stretch Ukraine's air defense further with every strike, forcing crews to spend scarce interceptors on yet another cheap target. The missile flies to its objective autonomously, and Russia claims a special flight profile designed to make it harder for air defense to spot and shoot down. A target drone becomes a weapon The Dan-T has an unusual pedigree. It began as the Dan-M, a jet-powered target drone Russia's Sokol bureau built in the early 1990s and imitated US Tomahawk cruise missiles for air-defense practice, now planned to be stripped of its recovery parachute, fitted with a warhead, and fired at Ukrainian cities. Like Russia's other new cruise weapons, it carries no operator link, steering itself by satellite and inertial navigation. The Banderol joins the list The Dan-T is not the only new weapon unsettling Ukraine's military. The experts named it alongside the S8000 Banderol, a separate cheap cruise missile that Russia already builds at up to 80 a month and has used in some of its heaviest strikes on Kyiv. The Dan-T closely resembles the Banderol and, being cheaper, may end up replacing it. Read also Europe gave Russia years to perfect its aerial killing. Ukraine is paying the price. Europe may be next. title: Three of four U.S. F-15E fighters lost during Operation Epic Fury were destroyed by friendly fire in Iran campaign, data show
body: The available information does not explain how the friendly-fire incidents occurred. It also does not identify the weapons involved, the locations of the losses or whether the crews were recovered. The losses came during an intensive air and ground campaign that began on February 28. U.S. forces struck approximately 13,500 targets, flew about 36,000 combat sorties and conducted more than 1,800 fire missions through April 7. The Pentagon had repositioned thousands of personnel and hundreds of advanced fighter aircraft in the months before combat operations started. At the height of the campaign, the U.S. force included more than a dozen fighter squadrons operating across the Central Command region. American aircraft targeted Iranian ballistic missile garrisons, air defense sites and facilities used to store cruise missiles and unmanned aircraft systems. The campaign also struck command centers, naval assets, mine-warfare capabilities and parts of Iran’s defense industrial base. The F-15E losses were part of a wider toll on U.S. military aviation during the operation. Dozens of American aircraft were destroyed or damaged by enemy action, friendly fire, accidents and incidents connected with combat search-and-rescue missions. Other recorded losses included an F-35A damaged by enemy fire over Iran and an A-10 destroyed after sustaining damage while returning from a combat search-and-rescue mission. Seven KC-135 tankers were also damaged or destroyed in a collision over Iraq and Iranian strikes on aircraft parked in Saudi Arabia. The Pentagon estimated equipment losses from Operation Epic Fury at $3.7 billion based on replacement costs. That figure was part of a wider $33.4 billion estimate for the campaign through late June. The F-15E losses were disclosed in Operation Epic Fury: Report to the United States Congress, April 1, 2026–June 30, 2026 . Its aircraft-loss table cited a Congressional Research Service assessment and subsequent vetting by U.S. Central Command.

title: Ukraine spent year ignoring one Russian drone-control tech, and now Geran-5 flies on it. President’s adviser warns next one, from space, is worse
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia's newest military satellites keep stalling short of orbit, and Ukraine's top technology adviser says that is exactly why no one should relax. Serhii Beskrestnov, the presidential adviser on defense technology known as Flash, warns that once Russia completes its "Rassvet" satellite network, Moscow could steer its Gerans and missiles from space, and that Ukraine has to build the jamming to stop it before that day comes. A working Rassvet would hand Russia a permanent link to its long-range weapons, letting it control drones and missiles online through satellites, what Flash calls "a small catastrophe." Russia is nowhere near that yet: it has launched around 32 satellites but needs 200 to 250 for stable, round-the-clock coverage, and its most recent batch stalled in low orbit. Flash's point is that the reprieve is temporary. "Russia is a space power," he wrote, and one heavy Angara rocket could loft much of the constellation in a single launch once its engines are fixed. Ukraine has tried to choke the program at its source, striking a Russian space-rocket plant in mid-August and reaching for the Plesetsk cosmodrome days later, though the effort has only slowed it. The MESH failure sets the warning His alarm rests on a mistake, he says, Ukraine already made. For a year, he wrote, no one in the armed forces systematically worked on countering the MESH radio networks Russia uses to fly its jet Gerans, and no one shielded the capital with electronic warfare, even as the enemy openly built out the technology. Breaking what he called a lifelong rule against criticizing colleagues, he "thanked" the former commander-in-chief and his electronic-warfare chief for the lapse, he wrote a bit earlier. The result, he said , is that Russian Geran-5 are now striking under MESH control while Ukrainian specialists scramble to catch up. The jamming must come first With Rassvet, Flash argues, Ukraine cannot afford the same delay. The counter-system must not only be designed but actually fielded before the constellation is up, with the country's key infrastructure shielded by the time Russia's satellites reach orbit. "This electronic warfare must ALREADY have closed all key infrastructure sites," he wrote. Building it, he cautioned, will be neither fast nor cheap. title: Russia has warned its cities about every strike for years. During the heaviest raid yet, on election day, it left the sirens silent
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian authorities left residents in and around Moscow without air raid sirens or phone alerts during Ukraine's largest combined strike on Moscow Oblast, apparently to guard turnout at Russia's parliamentary elections, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said . The silence angered residents and even pro-war commentators as a major oil refinery burned. For most of this war, Russia has handled strikes on its cities as a routine to be announced, warned about, and waited out. Withholding warnings during the heaviest raid yet, in the middle of a national vote, suggests authorities will trade residents' safety for the look of a calm election when a political milestone is on the line. Sirens stayed off during the biggest raid Ukraine hit strategic sites across the Moscow area overnight on 19-20 September, the last day of Russia's State Duma vote. Moscow Oblast officials did not switch on air alert sirens or send the SMS warnings they had used during far smaller attacks. They quietly restricted mobile service without major public notice. Ukraine struck oil and logistics targets, not polling stations, according to the experts, and authorities appeared to place high turnout above protecting civilians. Moscow Oblast residents complained that no alert reached them, some posting on the Telegram channel of regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov before it closed comments. A prominent Kremlin-linked military blogger attacked the official response, saying it erodes public trust and that cutting mobile service does "not really help." What the drones hit Ukraine's General Staff reported striking the Gazpromneft-Moscow Oil Refinery in the city's Kapotnya district, one of Russia's largest plants, causing a large fire. Ukrainian manufacturer Fire Point said its FP-1 drones completely shut down the refinery, with all primary processing units damaged. Governor Andrei Vorobyov claimed air defenses countered 249 drones across 17 municipal districts. The strike was part of Ukraine's widening campaign against the fuel sector funding Russia's war, with about a fifth of Russian refining capacity offline . title: Ukraine shut down this Samara refinery in June—now its drones are back, and both distillation units are burning again
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukrainian drones struck Rosneft's Kuibyshev refinery in Samara overnight on 22 September, hitting two primary crude-processing units and triggering a large fire, Ukrainian drone and missile maker Fire Point confirmed . The strike is part of Ukraine's ongoing campaign against the fuel infrastructure that sustains Russia's war—the same plant had to halt crude processing after a drone attack in June. The attack came one day after US President Donald Trump for the second time in a week urged Ukraine's leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to stop the refinery campaign. Ukraine strikes Russian refineries to degrade the fuel supply that funds and sustains Russia's invasion—every barrel of diesel or aviation fuel that never leaves a wrecked distillation column is a barrel that cannot power Russian tanks, aircraft, or export revenue. With nearly half of Russia's refining capacity now offline , the campaign has become one of Ukraine's most effective tools for raising the economic cost of the war. FP-1 drones hit both primary processing units Fire Point said its FP-1 drones struck the Kuibyshev refinery, hitting the AVT-4 and AVT-5 atmospheric-vacuum distillation units —the plant's primary crude-processing installations. A large fire broke out on the refinery grounds. The Kuibyshev refinery is part of Rosneft and has a designed processing capacity of about 7 million tons of crude oil per year. It is located more than 900 km from the war zone in Ukraine. Smoke from the Kuibyshev refinery fire seen from a residential neighborhood in Samara, 22 September 2026. Photo: Exilenova+ In 2024, the plant processed 4.7 million tons of crude and produced about 800,000 tons of gasoline, 1.4 million tons of diesel, and 1.3 million tons of fuel oil. Samara, moment of attack pic.twitter.com/U47yrene3z — Exilenova+ (@Exilenova_plus) September 22, 2026 Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ began reporting explosions and air defense activity in Samara Oblast at 3:50 a.m. By 4:24 a.m., the channel posted videos showing a night fire at the refinery. OSINT channel World Militaries identified the AVT-5 unit as the initial fire site. Geolocation of the Samara fire. Source: world.militares / Telegram Russian news Telegram channel Astra separately confirmed the fire at the Kuibyshev refinery. By morning, the fire was still burning. The smoke plume stretched about 100 km across Samara Oblast, Exilenova+ reported. Smoke from the Kuibyshev Oil Refinery in Samara has already stretched for 100 km across Russian territory. pic.twitter.com/U5KQ0v1eTW — Exilenova+ (@Exilenova_plus) September 22, 2026 The Kuibyshev refinery stopped processing crude in June 2026 after Ukrainian drones hit its AVT-4 and AVT-5 units—the same pair now struck again. Each unit processes about 10,000 tons of crude per day, or roughly 73,000 barrels. The refinery had also suspended operations after a drone attack in August 2025. Other targets in the overnight wave Exilenova+ also reported that Ukrainian forces struck a military base in the city of Pochep in Bryansk Oblast overnight, with fire observed at the site. Residents of Tolyatti in Samara Oblast reported explosions, and witnesses suggested the Tolyattikauchuk synthetic rubber plant had been hit, Suspilne reported. Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed the attack, claiming Russian air defenses intercepted "dozens of drones." He said drones "targeted industrial enterprises" but did not name which ones. Russia's Defense Ministry claimed 297 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over 14 oblasts and occupied Crimea. Black smoke from the Kuibyshev refinery fire seen from a highway near Samara, 22 September 2026. Photo: Exilenova+ Part of an ongoing campaign against Russian fuel infrastructure Ukraine's General Staff confirmed strikes on both the Bashneft-UNPZ refinery in Ufa and the Kuibyshev refinery in Samara, with fire observed at both sites. Ukraine has been striking Russian refineries continuously for months—hitting targets in Saratov and Volgograd on 11 September, Slavyansk-na-Kubani on 14 September, Syzran on 15 September, Yaroslavl on 17 September, and Ufa on 21 September, the night before the Kuibyshev strike. Earlier, the General Staff said the campaign has disabled 45% of Russia's oil-refining capacity. The strikes have also pushed Russia's fuel crisis into Central Asia, where shortages forced Kazakhstan to seek emergency supplies. Smoke plume from the Kuibyshev refinery fire seen from a high-rise in Samara, 22 September 2026. Photo: Exilenova+ Trump urged Zelenskyy to stop the campaign for the second time in a week during their 21 September call, telling him "don't hit diesel fuel" and blaming Ukrainian strikes—not the Iran conflict—for rising US diesel prices. Each plant hit again after a previous shutdown means Russia's repair cycle cannot keep up—the forced downtime compounds, diesel exports are already banned, and gasoline production is falling faster than alternative supply from Kazakhstan or anywhere else can replace it. Read also All three Rosneft Samara refineries now offline or reduced as drones halt Kuibyshevsky operations yesterday Ukraine keeps hitting the fuel that Russia’s war runs on. Its latest target is the Slavyansk-EKO refinery, with an annual processing capacity of at least 3 million tonnes Ukraine strikes Russia’s second-largest oil refinery again in major overnight attack, also hitting airfield and drone launch site

title: UK to support Saudi defensive operations in response to renewed Houthi attacks
body: The United Kingdom (UK) has agreed to assist Saudi Arabia with defensive operations in response to renewed Houthi attacks in the Gulf region. On September 22, 2026, the UK government confirmed that in the face of “escalating violence” it will provide an Royal Air Force (RAF) Voyager air-to-air refueling aircraft. The Ministry of Defense described both Saudi Arabia and Yemen as “long-standing partners” that “play a vital role in regional stability”. The development comes after Houthi rebels advanced in Yemen earlier this month, capturing the Red Sea port city of Mocha and other sections of the country’s coastline. RAF On September 20, 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, their targeting of civilian sites, and the threat these attacks pose to security and stability in the region. On September 22, 2026, Secretary of Defense Wes Streeting said: “The Houthis are a dangerous threat to regional stability and it is in the UK’s national economic and security interest that they do not succeed.” He added: “We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and are clear that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen.” In a statement the UK said that escalations in the Gulf region can have a “serious impact at home” with “increasing prices, disruption to energy supplies, and extra costs for British businesses”. A Royal Saudi Air Force F-15SA fighter. (Credit: Ronnie Macdonald / Wikimedia Commons) “It is in the UK’s national interest to protect regional stability, protect vital trade and energy supplies, and see a diplomatic resolution to the conflict in Yemen,” Streeting said. The support builds on the UK’s existing military contribution to Saudi Arabia’s air defense, including the deployment of air defense equipment and personnel helping to protect against missile and drone attacks. The Houthi rebels are closely aligned with Iran which has itself been locked in a conflict with the US and Israel. The conflict, along with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has caused global oil prices to surge, affecting the health of many national economies around the world. title: APDR Podcast Episode 154 with host Kym Bergmann
body: We begin with another Defence procurement farce. Two years ago Defence abandoned a project called JP 9102 for geostationary military communications satellites with Minister Richard Marles explaining that they were too vulnerable and of insufficient capability. In an extraordinary development, Defence has just issued a tender for a satellite very similar to the one they cancelled. The problem is that we have missed at least three years acquiring a vital capability – and Australian industry lost more than $300 million because of the ineptitude of Defence. The Middle East continues to unravel with Donald Trump now seeking to blame Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for high US diesel prices rather than his own stupid unprovoked war with Iran. At least Ukraine is hitting back with massive drone and ballistic missile attacks on Russia. This is demonstrating the future of warfare – mass attacks from these systems. Only now is the full extent of the damage Iran has caused to US facilities using similar weapons in the Persian Gulf region being revealed. It looks very much like Trump is abandoning US allies in the Middle East – especially Saudi Arabia. The Saudis and the Gulf monarchies believed that the US could be counted on as their security guarantor. The reality is that Trump is throwing them under the bus. Why do Australian politicians and Defence officials think we are any different? To listen to the podcast, click here . title: Ukraine’s defence ministry says forces neutralised over 350,000 Russian drones this year, including 31,000 Shaheds and 220,000 fixed-wing UAVs
body: Unmanned systems units accounted for more than 320,000 fixed-wing and copter-type UAVs. That total included about 220,000 fixed-wing drones and 100,000 copters. The ministry said another 31,000 Shahed drones were shot down by unmanned systems units, mobile fire groups and army aviation. It said each interception reduced the threat to Ukrainian troops and civilians. Ukraine uses DELTA to confirm engagements and collect operational data from the battlefield. The system allows forces to examine individual interceptions and expand successful methods more quickly. The destruction of fixed-wing drones limits Russia’s ability to conduct reconnaissance behind Ukrainian lines. It also disrupts strikes and the correction of long-range attacks against civilian targets, including critical infrastructure. Intercepting copter-type drones reduces Russia’s ability to locate and attack Ukrainian positions and equipment near the front. These UAVs pose a direct threat to troops and military assets in frontline areas. The scale of the effort increased sharply during the final month of summer. Ukrainian forces destroyed almost 24,000 copter-type drones and 35,000 fixed-wing UAVs in August alone.
